title: The Girl Who Was Afraid to Begin
summary: Wren wants to make something beautiful, but she is so afraid of doing it badly that she never begins at all. When a strange gardener gives her a seed that will only grow if planted imperfectly, she learns that a flawed beginning is the only kind there is — and that nothing finished was ever started perfectly.

chapters.title: The Blank Page
chapters.body:
Wren was eleven, and she had, everyone agreed, a great deal of talent — and not one finished thing to show for it.

She wanted to make beautiful things. She dreamed of them constantly: paintings, stories, carvings, songs. In her head, they were perfect — vivid and lovely and exactly right. But every time she sat down to actually make one, something stopped her cold. She would pick up the brush, or the pen, or the knife, and she would think: what if it comes out wrong? What if the real thing isn't as beautiful as the one in my head? What if I begin, and the first stroke is clumsy, and I ruin it? And the fear of doing it badly grew so large that she couldn't do it at all. She would set down the brush. She would leave the page blank. She would keep the beautiful thing safe and perfect in her head, unmade, rather than risk making it imperfectly in the world.

Her room was full of the evidence. Blank canvases she'd never dared to paint. Empty notebooks she'd never dared to write in. Blocks of wood she'd never dared to carve, in case she carved them wrong. She had all the materials, and all the talent, and all the dreams — and nothing finished, nothing even started, because she could not bear to begin a thing badly, and she had somehow convinced herself that if she couldn't begin it perfectly, she shouldn't begin it at all.

It made her deeply unhappy, though she hid it. She watched other children make things — clumsy things, flawed things, things far less lovely than the visions in her own head — and she watched them finish those things, and improve, and make better ones, while she sat with her blank pages and her perfect unmade dreams and made nothing at all. She told herself she was being careful. She told herself she was holding out for the beautiful thing she knew she could make. But underneath, she knew the truth: she was afraid, and the fear was winning, and she was wasting all her talent guarding it from the risk of being used imperfectly.

One grey afternoon, wandering unhappily past the edge of the village, Wren came upon a garden she'd never seen before — a wild, glorious, overgrown garden, bursting with flowers of every color, tended by a strange old gardener with dirt-black hands and a knowing smile. And the flowers were not perfect. That was the first thing Wren noticed. They were lopsided, some of them, and oddly colored, and grew at strange angles — and yet the garden as a whole was the most beautiful, alive, joyful thing she had ever seen, precisely because nothing in it was trying to be perfect.

The old gardener watched Wren stare at his flowers, and he seemed to see right through her, to the blank pages and the unmade dreams and the fear.

"You want to make something beautiful," he said. It wasn't a question. "But you're afraid to begin, because you're afraid it won't be as perfect as the picture in your head." He smiled, not unkindly. "I know that fear. I've seen it wither more talent than any drought ever killed. Come here, child. I have something for you."

chapters.title: The Seed That Grew Crooked
chapters.body:
The old gardener pressed a single seed into Wren's palm — small and brown and ordinary-looking — and closed her fingers around it.

"This is a special seed," he said. "It will grow into the most beautiful flower you've ever seen. But it has one strange condition, and you must understand it before you plant it." He fixed her with his knowing eyes. "This seed will only grow if you plant it imperfectly. If you try to plant it perfectly — if you wait for the perfect spot, the perfect moment, the perfect way, and try to do it exactly right — it will not grow at all. It will sit in the ground, safe and unbegun, forever. It grows only when planted by a hand willing to plant it wrong. Do you understand?"

Wren did not understand, not really, and she said so.

"You will," said the gardener. "Go home. Plant it. But here is the rule: you must plant it today, before the sun sets, in whatever spot you happen to choose, in whatever way you happen to manage — knowing it might be the wrong spot, and the wrong way, and that you might do it badly. That is the only way it grows. Now go."

So Wren took the seed home, and she prepared to plant it — and at once, she felt the old familiar fear rise up. She stood in her garden with the seed in her hand, and she thought: but where's the perfect spot? What if I plant it in the wrong place, and it doesn't get enough sun? What if I plant it too deep, or not deep enough? What if I do it wrong and ruin it? And she found herself frozen, exactly as she always froze before a blank page — unable to begin, wanting to wait until she was sure she could do it perfectly, wanting to hold the seed safe and unplanted rather than risk planting it badly.

The sun sank lower. And Wren understood, standing there paralyzed with the seed in her hand, that this was the whole test. The seed would only grow if she planted it imperfectly — which meant the seed would only grow if she was brave enough to begin without being sure, to act without a guarantee, to plant it in a spot that might be wrong, in a way that might be clumsy, and accept that it might not come out perfect. The very fear that had kept all her pages blank was the exact thing standing between her and the flower. If she waited for perfect, the seed would die unplanted, just as all her dreams had died unmade. The only way to grow the beautiful thing was to risk growing it badly.

And the sun was setting.

So Wren, with her heart pounding, did the thing she had never let herself do. She stopped looking for the perfect spot. She knelt down in an ordinary patch of earth — not sure it was the right one — and she dug a hole with her hands, not sure it was the right depth, and she put the seed in, not sure she was doing it right, and she covered it over, imperfectly, clumsily, without any guarantee at all. She planted it wrong, or maybe right — she couldn't know — and that was exactly the point. She had begun. Badly, unsurely, imperfectly. But she had begun.

And the next morning, a green shoot had pushed up out of the ordinary patch of earth, reaching for the sun.

chapters.title: The Only Kind of Beginning
chapters.body:
The seed grew — and it grew, Wren noticed, a little crooked, leaning at an odd angle, not at all the perfect straight stem she might have pictured. And yet it grew, and budded, and one morning it bloomed into a flower so strange and vivid and alive and beautiful that Wren gasped to see it. It was not a perfect flower. It was lopsided, and its colors were unexpected, and it leaned. And it was the most beautiful thing she had ever made grow, precisely because she had been brave enough to plant it imperfectly instead of never planting it at all.

She went back to the strange gardener's garden to thank him, and to tell him the seed had grown, and the old man smiled his knowing smile.

"Of course it grew," he said. "You planted it. That's all it ever needed. Not perfect planting — just planting. A beginning, however clumsy." He gestured at his glorious, imperfect, overgrown garden. "Do you see now? Every flower here grew the same way. Not one of them was planted perfectly. Not one of them grew straight and flawless. They grew because someone was willing to plant them wrong, and let them grow crooked, and love them anyway. That's the only kind of beautiful there is, child. The kind that was begun imperfectly, by someone brave enough to begin."

And Wren understood, at last, the thing the seed had been sent to teach her. There is no such thing as a perfect beginning. Every finished, beautiful thing in all the world — every painting and story and carving and song, every flower and garden — was started imperfectly, by someone who didn't know if they were doing it right, who risked doing it badly, who made a clumsy first stroke and kept going anyway. The perfect version in your head is not the real thing; it's just the dream of the thing. And the only way to turn a dream into something real is to begin it badly — because beginning badly is the only way anyone has ever begun anything. The blank page stays perfect and beautiful and safe forever, and produces nothing. The marked page, clumsy and flawed and begun, is the only page that can ever become a masterpiece.

Wren went home, and she looked at all her blank canvases and empty notebooks and uncarved blocks of wood — all her perfect, safe, unbegun dreams — and for the first time she understood that they were not treasures she was protecting. They were flowers she was refusing to plant. And she picked up a brush, and she stood before a blank canvas, and the old fear rose up — what if it comes out wrong? — and this time, she remembered the crooked flower, and she smiled, and she thought: it will come out wrong. That's how it comes out at all. And she made the first stroke.

It was clumsy. The first stroke was clumsy, and the second, and the whole first painting she made was lopsided and flawed and not nearly as beautiful as the vision in her head. And Wren finished it anyway — the first thing she had ever finished — and then she made another, a little better, and another, better still. Because that is the secret the perfect never learn and the brave discover: you get better only by beginning badly, over and over, and finishing the flawed thing, and beginning again. The ones who wait to begin perfectly never begin, and so never improve, and so never make anything at all. The ones who are brave enough to begin badly are the only ones who ever, in the end, make anything good.

Wren became, in time, a maker of genuinely beautiful things — paintings and carvings and stories that people treasured. But she never forgot the crooked flower, and she never again waited for a perfect beginning, because she knew there was no such thing. And when she grew old, and young people with great talent and blank pages came to her, frozen by the fear of doing it badly, she would give them a single strange seed, and tell them it would only grow if planted imperfectly, and send them home to learn the thing she had learned: that a flawed beginning is the only kind of beginning there is, and that nothing beautiful was ever made by anyone too afraid to begin it badly. The blank page is not safety. It is the one place where nothing can ever grow. And the crooked, clumsy, imperfect first stroke — made by a trembling, unsure, brave hand — is where every beautiful thing in the world has always started.
